summary_paragraph: A man with a history of non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction 20%), COPD, type I diabetes, and prior crack cocaine use was admitted for acute on chronic systolic heart failure triggered by dietary sodium indiscretion. He presented with progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, and cough with frothy sputum. Initial evaluation revealed hypoxia, elevated BNP, and bilateral pulmonary opacities on imaging. He was treated with IV furosemide for aggressive diuresis, resulting in a weight loss from 201 to 193 lbs. Due to persistent respiratory distress, he was briefly monitored in the ICU but did not require mechanical ventilation. Antibiotics and steroids were discontinued after no evidence of infection or acute pneumonitis was found. His carvedilol was reduced due to blood pressure concerns, and lasix was increased to 40 mg twice daily at discharge. He improved clinically, ambulating independently on room air, and was discharged home with instructions on daily weight monitoring, low-sodium diet, and follow-up for cardiology and hepatitis C management.
